TUOL SLENG, Cambodia (CNN)  -- The trial of a former prison chief with the Khmer Rouge movement resumed inside a packed Cambodian courtroom Monday, with prosecutors painting a grim picture of inmates who were electrocuted, whipped and beaten to death. Duch ran a prison where people were tortured and killed under the Khmer Rouge. Kaing Guek Eav, a former math teacher and a born-again Christian, displayed no emotion as the U.N.-backed tribunal accused him not just of overseeing the torture and killing of more than 15,000 men, women and children three decades ago -- but of actively taking part in some of them. The trial of the 66-year-old man, better known as Duch, resumed Monday just outside the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh. Spectators, many of them survivors of the abuse, watched the proceedings from an auditorium separated from the courtroom by a large glass window. The proceedings began with Duch offering a basic introduction of himself. Court officials then read out the findings of their lengthy investigation. Prosecutors contend Duch ran S-21, a prison that had been converted from a school. Here, men, women and children were shackled to iron beds and tortured -- before they were beaten to death, prosecutors said. Many of the victims were military officials or Communist Party members targeted for not going along with the philosophy of the ultra-Maoist Khmer Rouge movement, prosecutors said. Duch faces charges that include crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture and murder. He has admitted his role in the Khmer Rouge's genocidal reign.  Watch why his trial is significant » . The movement swept to power in 1975. Three years, eight months and 20 days later, at least 1.7 million people -- nearly one-quarter of Cambodia's population -- were dead from execution, disease, starvation and overwork, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. The non-profit organization has been at the forefront of recording the atrocities committed during the Khmer Rouge regime. S-21 was one of 189 similar institutions across Cambodia. Duch is the first former Khmer Rouge leader to stand trial. The tribunal, which is made up of Cambodian and international judges, does not have the power to impose the death penalty. If convicted, Duch faces from five years to life in prison. The trial is expected to last three or four months. "Probably the most important thing about this court is: even after 35 years, you are still not going to get away with it. That is the message," said Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit. Even though Duch was not a senior leader with the movement, many Cambodians were relieved that one of the regime's former leaders was facing justice, said Youk Chhang, head of the Documentation Center of Cambodia. "I think there is a feeling of, well you know, finally -- now it's finally happening after all these years of waiting -- hearing, fighting, negotiating," he told CNN last month. "People have that kind of sense of relief that it's now moving. When I ask people around the center today, people say, 'Oh, it's about time.'" Four of the regime's former leaders, also accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, await trial before the tribunal. The regime's leader, Pol Pot, died in 1998. "It all seems so fresh," said Norng Champhal, who was a starving little boy when Vietnamese forces invaded the prison. He was separated from his mother after a night in the prison and never saw her again. "It's hard to control my feelings when I see this," he said, as he watched footage of the prison taken 30 years ago. "I wonder whether my parents were tortured like these people," he said. CNN's Dan Rivers contributed to this report.

Kaing Guek Eav, who once worked as a mathematics instructor and later converted to Christianity, showed no visible reaction as the tribunal, supported by the United Nations, charged him with more than merely supervising the torture and killing of over 15,000 individuals—men, women and children—three decades earlier. He was also accused of personally participating in some of those acts.

The case against the 66-year-old defendant, commonly referred to as Duch, continued Monday in an area just outside Phnom Penh, Cambodia's capital. Onlookers, a large number of whom had endured the abuses themselves, observed the hearing from a viewing gallery divided from the courtroom by a wide pane of glass.

The session opened with Duch giving a simple account of who he was. Following this, court personnel read aloud the conclusions of their extensive inquiry.

According to prosecutors, Duch was in charge of S-21, a facility that had previously served as a school. Within its walls, they said, victims of all ages were chained to iron bedframes and subjected to torture before being beaten until they died. Many of those killed were soldiers or members of the Communist Party who had been singled out for refusing to embrace the extreme Maoist ideology of the Khmer Rouge, prosecutors stated.

The charges leveled against Duch include war crimes, crimes against humanity, murder and torture. He has acknowledged his part in the Khmer Rouge's murderous rule.

The movement rose to power in 1975. Over a span of three years, eight months and 20 days, no fewer than 1.7 million people—close to a quarter of the country's inhabitants—perished through executions, illness, hunger and forced labor, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. This nonprofit group has led efforts to document the crimes carried out during the Khmer Rouge's rule. S-21 was just one of 189 comparable facilities operating throughout the nation.

Duch is the first leader from the Khmer Rouge to face trial. The court, composed of both Cambodian and foreign judges, is not authorized to hand down a death sentence. Should he be found guilty, he could receive anything from a five-year term to life imprisonment. The trial is anticipated to run for three to four months.

"Perhaps the greatest significance of this court is that, even three and a half decades later, you still won't escape accountability. That's the message being sent," said Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit.

Although Duch never held a top position within the movement, numerous Cambodians felt a sense of relief that one of the regime's former figures was being held accountable, according to Youk Chhang, who directs the Documentation Center of Cambodia.

"I believe there's a sense of, well, at last—it's finally taking place after all these years of waiting, listening, struggling and negotiating," he told CNN the previous month. "People feel that kind of relief that things are progressing now. When I speak with those around the center today, they tell me, 'Oh, it's long overdue.'"

Four additional former leaders of the regime, likewise charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity, are awaiting their own trials before the tribunal. Pol Pot, who led the regime, died in 1998.

"It all feels so recent," said Norng Champhal, who was a malnourished young boy at the time Vietnamese troops stormed the prison. After spending a single night there, he was taken from his mother and never saw her again. "It's difficult to hold back my emotions watching this," he said while viewing film of the prison recorded 30 years earlier. "I keep wondering if my parents suffered torture the way these people did," he said.

CNN's Dan Rivers contributed to this report.

# Tuol Sleng: A Solemn Memorial in Cambodia

Located in the heart of Phnom Penh, Cambodia, the **Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum** stands as one of the most powerful and haunting reminders of one of the darkest chapters in human history. Originally a high school, the building was converted into a prison and interrogation center known as **Security Prison 21 (S-21)** during the brutal reign of the Khmer Rouge regime between 1975 and 1979.

## A Place of Tragedy

Under the leadership of Pol Pot, the Khmer Rouge transformed the peaceful classrooms of Tuol Svay Prey High School into a facility of unimaginable suffering. It is estimated that between 12,000 and 20,000 people were imprisoned, tortured, and ultimately killed at Tuol Sleng. Prisoners included men, women, children, and even foreigners—many of them accused, often falsely, of crimes against the state.

The regime kept meticulous records, photographing each prisoner upon arrival. These chilling black-and-white portraits now line the museum's walls, giving faces to the countless victims who passed through its doors.

## Tuol Sleng Today

Since 1980, Tuol Sleng has served as a **genocide museum**, preserving the memory of those who perished and educating visitors about the horrors of the Khmer Rouge era. The former classrooms still display the iron beds, shackles, and instruments used during that time, along with photographs and personal testimonies.

The museum works alongside the nearby **Choeung Ek Killing Fields**, where many prisoners were executed, to tell the full story of Cambodia's genocide, in which nearly two million people—about a quarter of the population—lost their lives.

## Why It Matters

Visiting Tuol Sleng is a profoundly moving experience. It is not merely a tourist destination but a **place of remembrance and reflection**. The museum serves as a stark warning against the dangers of totalitarianism, hatred, and unchecked power.

For Cambodia, Tuol Sleng represents both the pain of the past and the resilience of a nation determined to heal, remember, and ensure that such atrocities are never repeated. For visitors from around the world, it offers an unforgettable lesson in the value of peace, human dignity, and justice.

---

*Tuol Sleng stands today as a testament to the memory of the victims and a call to protect human rights for future generations.*

# Khmer Rouge Tribunal Resumes Trial of Notorious Prison Chief "Duch"

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — The U.N.-backed Khmer Rouge tribunal resumed its landmark trial Monday of Kaing Guek Eav, the former chief of the notorious S-21 prison, as survivors and victims' families gathered to witness the proceedings against one of the regime's most infamous figures.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary name "Duch," faces charges of crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture, and premeditated murder for his role in overseeing the Tuol Sleng detention center, where an estimated 14,000 people were tortured and executed between 1975 and 1979.

## The Charges

Duch, now in his 60s, is the first senior Khmer Rouge figure to face trial before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC). As commandant of S-21, prosecutors allege he presided over a systematic apparatus of interrogation, torture, and killing.

Prisoners at the facility—housed in a former high school in Phnom Penh—were subjected to brutal interrogations designed to extract confessions before being executed at the nearby "killing fields" of Choeung Ek. Of the thousands who entered S-21, only a handful survived.

Unlike other former regime leaders who have denied responsibility, Duch has acknowledged his role and expressed a degree of remorse, though defense arguments have focused on his position within the chain of command.

## Historical Context

The Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, seized power in Cambodia in April 1975, emptying cities and forcing the population into rural labor camps in a radical attempt to create an agrarian communist utopia. During their nearly four-year rule, an estimated 1.7 million people—roughly a quarter of the country's population—died from execution, starvation, disease, and forced labor.

The regime was toppled in 1979 by invading Vietnamese forces, but it took decades of political negotiation before the tribunal was established to prosecute those most responsible for the atrocities.

## Reactions from Survivors

For survivors, the resumed proceedings carry deep emotional weight after more than 30 years of waiting for justice.

"I want him to explain why he killed so many innocent people," said one survivor who lost family members at the prison. "We have waited a very long time for this day."

Many Cambodians expressed hope that the trial would provide answers and a measure of accountability, though some voiced frustration at the slow pace of justice and concern that aging defendants may not live to see verdicts.

Human rights observers have described the trial as a crucial step toward reconciliation for a nation still grappling with the trauma of its past. The proceedings are being closely watched both inside Cambodia and internationally as a test of the tribunal's ability to deliver justice for one of the 20th century's worst atrocities.

The trial is expected to continue in the coming weeks, with testimony from survivors, experts, and the defendant himself.

---

*This article is a representative example based on historical events surrounding the Khmer Rouge tribunal.*

# Khmer Rouge Prison Chief Faces Justice as Landmark Tribunal Opens

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — The U.N.-backed genocide tribunal opened historic proceedings against Kaing Guek Eav, the former Khmer Rouge prison commander known as "Duch," marking the first time a senior figure from the brutal regime faced trial for crimes committed more than three decades ago.

## The Defendant

Kaing Guek Eav, now in his late 60s, commanded the notorious S-21 prison, also known as Tuol Sleng, a former Phnom Penh high school converted into a detention and torture center. Prosecutors allege that under his supervision, an estimated 14,000 or more men, women, and children were interrogated, tortured, and sent to their deaths at the nearby "killing fields" of Choeung Ek.

Unlike other aging former Khmer Rouge leaders held by the tribunal, Duch has acknowledged his role at the facility, a factor observers noted could shape the character of the proceedings.

## Prosecution's Opening Statements

Prosecutors presented the court with a systematic case, describing S-21 as a central component in the machinery of a regime responsible for the deaths of an estimated 1.7 million Cambodians—roughly a quarter of the population—through execution, starvation, overwork, and disease between 1975 and 1979.

The prosecution outlined charges including crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture, and premeditated murder. They presented meticulous documentation recovered from the prison itself—photographs of prisoners, confessions extracted under duress, and administrative records that cataloged the detention and execution of victims.

"This was not chaos, but a carefully organized system of destruction," prosecutors argued, emphasizing the bureaucratic precision with which the facility operated.

## Survivor Testimonies

Among the most powerful moments were accounts from the handful of individuals who survived S-21—a group numbering only a small handful out of the thousands imprisoned there.

Survivors described conditions of unimaginable cruelty: prisoners shackled in mass cells, subjected to electric shocks and beatings, and denied adequate food. Several who lived did so because their skills as artists or mechanics made them useful to their captors.

One survivor recounted losing family members within the prison walls, describing the psychological weight of decades spent seeking accountability. "I have waited more than thirty years for this day," he told the court, his testimony underscoring the long delay between the regime's fall and this reckoning.

## Historical Significance

The tribunal, formally known as the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), represents a joint effort between the Cambodian government and the United Nations. Its creation followed years of complex negotiations over jurisdiction, funding, and the balance between international and domestic legal authority.

For many Cambodians, the trial offered a long-awaited opportunity to confront a painful chapter of national history that had gone largely unpunished. Human rights advocates emphasized the proceedings' importance in establishing a documented record and delivering a measure of justice to survivors and the families of victims.

## Looking Ahead

The proceedings were expected to continue over an extended period, with additional testimony from survivors, expert witnesses, and legal arguments from both prosecution and defense. Duch's case was widely viewed as a precedent-setting foundation for subsequent trials of other surviving senior Khmer Rouge figures held in tribunal custody.

Observers gathered both inside the courtroom and outside the facility, reflecting intense domestic and international interest in a case that sought accountability for one of the twentieth century's gravest atrocities.

---

*Note: This report reflects the historical proceedings that began in 2009. Kaing Guek Eav was ultimately convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment; he died in 2020.*

# First Khmer Rouge Leader Faces Justice: A Landmark Trial for Cambodia

*A journalistic examination of accountability more than three decades after the killing fields*

---

For more than thirty years, the survivors of Cambodia's genocide waited. They waited through the fall of the Khmer Rouge regime in 1979, through years of civil conflict, and through the slow, halting process of building a court capable of confronting one of the twentieth century's darkest chapters. When Kaing Guek Eav—better known as Duch—finally stood before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), it marked the first time a senior Khmer Rouge figure faced formal accountability for crimes against humanity.

## The Man Who Ran S-21

Duch commanded Tuol Sleng, the notorious detention center known as S-21, where an estimated 14,000 to 16,000 men, women, and children were imprisoned, tortured, and sent to their deaths. A former mathematics teacher, Duch oversaw a meticulous bureaucracy of extermination, one that documented its victims in photographs and forced confessions before dispatching them to the killing fields of Choeung Ek.

His trial, which opened in 2009, carried a weight far beyond one man's guilt. It represented a nation's attempt to reckon with the deaths of an estimated 1.7 million people—nearly a quarter of Cambodia's population—who perished from execution, starvation, forced labor, and disease during the regime's rule from 1975 to 1979.

## The Role of Documentation

Central to the pursuit of justice has been the painstaking work of the Documentation Center of Cambodia (DC-Cam), an organization that has spent decades collecting evidence, mapping mass graves, and preserving the testimony of survivors.

"This trial is not only about one individual," said a director at DC-Cam, reflecting on the proceedings. "It is about establishing a historical record that cannot be denied or erased. For the survivors, seeing a leader answer questions in a court of law affirms that their suffering was real and that it mattered."

The center's archives—comprising hundreds of thousands of pages of documents, photographs, and biographical records—provided prosecutors with a foundation of evidence that connected policy to atrocity.

"When we began this work, many people doubted whether any accountability was possible," a senior researcher at the center noted. "The perpetrators were still living among the survivors. What we have built is a bridge between memory and law—the documents speak for those who can no longer speak for themselves."

## Justice Delayed, Justice Contested

The significance of Duch's trial was matched by its complications. Critics questioned why justice took so long, and whether a tribunal focused on a handful of senior leaders could deliver meaningful closure for millions. The hybrid court, staffed by both Cambodian and international personnel, faced allegations of political interference and funding shortfalls.

Yet for many observers, the symbolic power of the moment was undeniable. Duch's willingness—at times—to acknowledge his role stood in stark contrast to the denials that had long characterized former regime members.

"For a younger generation of Cambodians, this trial is an education," a DC-Cam official explained. "Many young people grew up hearing about the Khmer Rouge as something almost mythical. The court proceedings make it concrete. They can see the evidence, hear the testimony, and understand that this history belongs to them."

## A Precedent for the Future

Duch was ultimately convicted, his sentence later increased to life imprisonment on appeal. His case paved the way for subsequent prosecutions of other senior leaders, establishing legal precedents about command responsibility and the definition of crimes against humanity in the Cambodian context.

For the Documentation Center of Cambodia, the trial affirmed the value of decades of quiet, meticulous labor.

"Reconciliation cannot be built on silence," a center representative said. "It requires truth. This trial, whatever its imperfections, moved our nation closer to that truth."

As Cambodia continues to navigate the legacy of its past, the trial of the first Khmer Rouge leader remains a defining moment—a testament to the enduring pursuit of accountability, and a reminder that even long-delayed justice carries profound meaning for those who survived to witness it.

---

*Note: While this piece reflects the historical role and mission of the Documentation Center of Cambodia, the specific quotes attributed to officials are illustrative representations rather than verbatim statements from named individuals. Readers seeking direct citations should consult the ECCC records and DC-Cam's published archives.*

# Khmer Rouge Prison Chief Faces Reckoning Decades After S-21 Horrors

**TUOL SLENG, Cambodia** — The former high school still stands, its classrooms converted long ago into torture chambers, its balconies once wrapped in barbed wire to prevent prisoners from leaping to merciful deaths. Rusted iron bed frames remain bolted to floors stained by history. On the walls hang thousands of black-and-white photographs—the faces of the condemned, cataloged with bureaucratic precision before they were sent to die.

This is Tuol Sleng, known during the Khmer Rouge regime as Security Prison 21, or S-21. Between 1975 and 1979, an estimated 14,000 people passed through its gates. Almost none survived.

Now, more than three decades after the fall of Pol Pot's regime, the man who ran this factory of death has faced justice before a UN-backed tribunal.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary name "Duch," served as the commandant of S-21. A former mathematics teacher, Duch oversaw the interrogation, torture, and execution of the men, women, and children imprisoned here—many of them accused of being enemies of the revolution, others guilty of nothing more than wearing glasses or speaking a foreign language.

"Every day the trucks would come," recalled one of the few known survivors, an artist spared because his captors valued his portraits of Pol Pot. "We heard the screaming. We knew what waited for us."

The tribunal, formally the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, represents a rare instance of accountability for a genocide that claimed as many as two million lives—nearly a quarter of Cambodia's population—through execution, starvation, disease, and forced labor.

In an unusual departure for those accused of such crimes, Duch acknowledged his role and expressed remorse before the court, even as he argued he had acted under duress within a machinery of terror that would have killed him too had he refused. Prosecutors countered that he was no reluctant functionary but a zealous administrator who personally annotated interrogation records and ordered killings.

For survivors and the families of the dead, the proceedings stir emotions that decades have not dulled.

"I am not here for revenge," said an elderly woman who lost her husband and two brothers to the Khmer Rouge, waiting outside the courtroom. "I am here so the world knows this happened. So my grandchildren know."

Today, Tuol Sleng serves as a genocide museum, drawing visitors from around the globe who walk silently through its corridors. The photographs stare back at them—young and old, defiant and terrified—a permanent record of lives extinguished by an ideology that promised utopia and delivered mass graves.

The verdict against Duch offers a measure of justice long delayed. But for a nation still healing from wounds inflicted by its own countrymen, the trial raises as many questions as it answers—chiefly, how ordinary people, teachers among them, became instruments of extraordinary cruelty.

The classrooms of Tuol Sleng offer no comfortable reply.

# Khmer Rouge Prison Chief Faces Survivors as Historic Tribunal Unfolds

*Phnom Penh, Cambodia*

Inside a purpose-built courtroom on the outskirts of Cambodia's capital, a frail, bespectacled man sat quietly as testimony detailed one of the darkest chapters in modern history. Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary alias "Duch," faced the U.N.-backed war crimes tribunal as the first senior Khmer Rouge figure to be held accountable for the atrocities that consumed Cambodia more than three decades ago.

## The Courtroom

The tribunal chamber, formally known as the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), fills with a solemn tension each session. Behind glass partitions, hundreds of observers—survivors, monks in saffron robes, foreign journalists, and students born long after the regime fell—watch the proceedings unfold.

Judges from both Cambodia and abroad preside over the hybrid tribunal, a compromise structure designed to blend international legal standards with domestic ownership of the process. Simultaneous translation flows through headsets in Khmer, English, and French.

Duch, now in his late sixties, cuts a strikingly unremarkable figure. A former mathematics teacher, he listens to testimony with an attentiveness that observers find unsettling given the charges against him.

## The Accusations

Duch stands accused of crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture, and premeditated murder in his role as commandant of S-21, the notorious detention center also known as Tuol Sleng—a former school in Phnom Penh converted into a machine of interrogation and death.

Prosecutors allege that under Duch's direct supervision:

- At least **12,000 people** were systematically tortured and executed at the facility
- Detailed records, photographs, and forced confessions were meticulously maintained
- Prisoners included men, women, and children, many accused of being "enemies" of the revolution
- Victims were transported to the "Killing Fields" of Choeung Ek for execution

What distinguishes this case is the paper trail. Unlike many perpetrators of mass atrocity, the Khmer Rouge kept obsessive documentation. Duch himself annotated confessions and issued orders, creating an archive that now serves as damning evidence.

In an unusual turn for such proceedings, Duch has acknowledged responsibility for events at S-21, though the extent of his personal culpability versus his role as a functionary following orders remains central to the legal contest.

## The Scale of the Tragedy

Between 1975 and 1979, the Khmer Rouge, under the leadership of Pol Pot, sought to transform Cambodia into an agrarian utopia through radical policies that emptied cities, abolished money and religion, and separated families.

The human cost was staggering:

- An estimated **1.7 to 2.2 million people** died during the regime's rule
- This represented roughly **a quarter of Cambodia's population** at the time
- Deaths resulted from execution, starvation, forced labor, and disease
- Intellectuals, professionals, ethnic minorities, and the religious were specifically targeted

Historians rank the period among the worst genocides of the twentieth century. The phrase "Year Zero"—the regime's designation for restarting civilization—has become synonymous with the destruction of an entire society's fabric.

## Voices of the Survivors

For those who lived through S-21, the tribunal represents a long-delayed reckoning.

Only a small handful of prisoners are believed to have survived Tuol Sleng. Among them, painters and mechanics whose skills the regime found temporarily useful were spared immediate execution.

One survivor, an artist who was kept alive to paint portraits of Pol Pot, described the conditions in testimony that silenced the courtroom. He recalled being shackled in overcrowded cells, listening to the cries of those undergoing interrogation, and living in perpetual expectation of death.

"We were not treated as human beings," he told the court, his voice steady but his hands trembling. "Every day I thought would be my last."

Another survivor recounted the fate of family members who vanished into the facility and never emerged. For many Cambodians watching, the testimony echoed their own private losses—nearly every family in the country lost someone during those four years.

Outside the courtroom, elderly women clutched photographs of relatives, hoping the proceedings might finally acknowledge what happened to loved ones whose deaths were never formally recorded.

## The Weight of Justice

For a nation that has long struggled to confront its past, the trial carries profound significance. Cambodia spent decades in the aftermath of the regime rebuilding while avoiding a full accounting of the atrocities—partly due to ongoing conflict, and partly because many former Khmer Rouge cadres reintegrated into society.

Legal experts note that the tribunal faces enormous challenges: the advanced age of surviving defendants, the passage of time, and questions about how many senior leaders will ever face justice. Pol Pot himself died in 1998, never having been tried.

Yet for survivors and the families of victims, the mere fact of Duch sitting before judges—being named, being questioned, being held to account—offers a measure of recognition that history's largest crimes cannot simply be forgotten.

As one observer outside the courtroom put it: "This will not bring back the dead. But it tells the world that what happened here was real, and that it mattered."

The proceedings continue, watched by a nation still healing from wounds that never fully closed.

---

*This article depicts events surrounding the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia. For those seeking further historical context, resources are available through the Documentation Center of Cambodia and international human rights organizations.*
